newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN human rights observers attacked in Rwanda.
newsitem.headline: UN human rights observers attacked in Rwanda.

text.p: Armed men, some in army uniforms, attacked two U.N. human rights observers in a remote Rwandan village, threw a grenade into their car, threatened to kill them and forced them to flee on foot, the U.N. said on Wednesday.

The United Nations Human Rights Office in Geneva said the two, a Briton and an Italian, were not seriously hurt during the daylight attack on January 13 in the village of Giciye in Gisenyi region near the troubled northwestern border with Zaire.
The U.N. Human Rights office, which has some 120 observers stationed in the tiny central African country, said in a statement it had temporarily suspended its work in Gisenyi.

It said the attackers were suspected to be members of armed opposition groups -- possibly referring to majority Hutu rebels fighting to topple the Tutsi-led government that took power after 1994's Hutu-led genocide of minority Tutsis.

The observers were attacked when they were meeting a commune official during a routine field visit to Giciye, a predominantly Hutu village and a hotspot in the guerrilla war between the rebels and Rwanda's Tutsi-dominated army.

A group of 10 unidentified men, eight armed with guns, two carrying grenades and some in military uniforms, entered the officials' bureau during the meeting and pushed the two observers and their translator out, the U.N. statement said.
The gunmen later forced the three to lie down and beat and robbed them in the presence of a group of local residents.

The observers were told to leave and threatened with death if they came back. They fled the area on foot after the gunmen tossed a grenade into their car and set fire to the engine, the U.N. statement said.

It was the most serious security incident targetting expatriates in Rwanda since the beating of three Western investigators of the U.N. genocide tribunal -- two Dutchmen and an American -- by government soldiers in January 1996.
Thousands of humanitarian workers flocked to Rwanda after the genocide of half a million Tutsis and allied Hutus.
Cars of U.N. staff and Western aid workers are sometimes stolen by soldiers and there are many robberies but reports of violence targetting foreigners are rare.
